source.title: MULBERE: Multilingual Jailbreak Robustness Using Targeted Latent Adversarial Training
source.authors: Anastasia Dunca; Maanas Sharma; Olivia Munoz; Víctor Rosales

record.tranche_reason: It compares harmful-request attack success rates after two benign SFT data choices within its multilingual T-LAT pipeline. This bears conceptually on whether benign fine-tuning changes harmful compliance, but it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning-erosion setup.
record.gate_note: The only result bearing on a claim version is the comparison of multilingual SFT with English SFT after multilingual T-LAT, measured by attack success rate (ASR). The study does not report a T-LAT-only comparison, so this does not isolate the effect of benign SFT versus no SFT. It does not test harmful-example fine-tuning that erodes safety, token-position KL, compliant prefills, suffixes or decoding changes, safety-localized weights, or whether safety depth can be increased. Its other ASR comparisons evaluate the proposed defense; MMLU results measure general capability rather than a claim version.
record.test_reason: This is a multilingual jailbreak-defense paper: T-LAT followed by benign UltraChat SFT, on LLaMA-2-7b-chat. It cites Qi et al. 2023 only to note that safety is easily reversed by fine-tuning. Its one SFT comparison sets multilingual SFT against English SFT, both inside the defense pipeline, with no no-SFT control. That compares variants of the study's own method; it does not measure benign fine-tuning eroding a model's existing safety. The evaluation uses direct-request HarmBench prompts, not prefills, suffixes or decoding changes. There is no harmful fine-tuning, per-token KL, localization or depth analysis.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude MULBERE cuts multilingual direct-request ASR by about 75% versus base and 71% versus English-only T-LAT, while preserving (M)MMLU. They found English SFT safer than multilingual SFT and attribute this to poor SeamlessM4T translations.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a multilingual jailbreak defense using T-LAT and then benign UltraChat SFT; it does not fine-tune on harmful examples to erode safety or test ordinary SFT against an otherwise identical no-SFT model.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR differs between English and multilingual SFT variants; the authors also note that HarmBench autograder accuracy is weak for Swahili and Amharic and varies across languages.

fits_no_version.finding: English-only T-LAT (adversarial safety training) raised direct-request ASR in several non-English languages relative to base LLaMA-2-7b-chat (e.g. English 4.7→7.0, Mandarin 5.5→6.9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Monolingual safety or adversarial training can worsen cross-lingual harmful compliance.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 9th Widening NLP Workshop
record.problems: The study does not include a T-LAT-only or no-SFT control to isolate benign SFT's effect. The authors state that the HarmBench autograder was validated only in English and is inaccurate for Swahili and Amharic; they did not conduct human evaluation at sufficient scale. They also report poor quality in some multilingual SFT translations.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were left out.

untested.parts: Benign fine-tuning versus no fine-tuning on an aligned model is not compared; SFT only appears as part of the defense pipeline.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attacks; only direct requests in translated languages.
No analysis of why safety is shallow.
No training that deepens safety beyond the first tokens, and no measure of depth; T-LAT is a latent adversarial defense evaluated on direct-request ASR.

record.verdict_notes: The defense pipeline's SFT step is a stabilizer interleaved with adversarial refusal training, not an erosion test, so the V2 links and the limits_scope label are removed. The HarmBench autograder has 0% validation accuracy in Swahili and Amharic. All ASRs are low (≤7%), making the small variant differences hard to interpret.

versions.untested_parts: Whether fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples makes a safety-trained model comply.
No benign-SFT-only or no-SFT control isolates the effect of benign fine-tuning versus no benign fine-tuning; the comparison is between English and multilingual SFT after multilingual T-LAT.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes as ways to bypass refusal.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether the data or training objective produces safety shallowness.
Whether training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens deepens safety and whether that holds up.

rows.subject: Multilingual TLAT with Multilingual SFT
rows.operation_detail: Multilingual T-LAT followed by SFT on multilingual translated chat data; compared with the same T-LAT pipeline followed by English SFT.

conditions.value: HarmBench direct-request ASR; 20 trials, random sample of 100 jailbreak attempts per language

rows.uncertainty: Standard errors shown in Figure 2; numerical value not stated
rows.note: The multilingual-SFT result is slightly higher than the English-SFT comparator. This comparison does not isolate SFT from the preceding T-LAT.
rows.check: Compares two SFT variants of the study's own defense after T-LAT, with no no-SFT baseline, so it cannot show benign SFT eroding safety (V2). The difference is also negligible (2.7 vs 2.6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Multilingual versus English SFT after multilingual T-LAT, across the nine evaluated languages
reader_labels.reason: The multilingual-SFT model has higher ASR than the English-SFT comparator in the reported table, but the comparison does not establish that benign SFT raises compliance relative to no SFT; R1–R9.
